summary: Describes a simple method for encoding telephone numbers in the local part of email addresses, with an extension mechanism for extra attributes for gateways to telephone-based services.

eli5.summary: It lets you write a phone number as an email address so mail can reach a phone service.

questions: how to put a phone number in an email address
what is a service selector in gstn email
subtitle: A minimal way to write a telephone number inside an email address, with a registered extension mechanism.

tldr.problem: Email-to-telephone gateways each used their own way to write a phone number as an email address, so there was no common format.
tldr.mechanism: The local part of the email address holds a service selector, an equals sign and a global phone number starting with +, plus optional /keyword=value extensions, all in front of the gateway's domain name.
tldr.outcome: It gives implementors one minimal format and a registration process for new service selectors and extension keywords. It obsoletes RFC 2303 with no technical or major changes and updates RFC 2846.

today: RFC 3191 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2303 and updates RFC 2846. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
The left-hand side (local-part) of an address made under this specification is not interpreted by anything except the MTA that handles mail for the domain on the right-hand side. Since the first email to GSTN (Global Switched Telephone Network) gateways appeared, implementors used many different ways to write a GSTN address as an email address. This memo describes the MINIMAL addressing method and the standard extension mechanism for defining more elements.

Implementations that support GSTN over email MUST support at least this specification. The opposite problem, letting a numeric-only telephone user reach email, is not discussed, and the full complexity of converting GSTN addressing is out of scope.

The RFC defines three terms: an I-pstn device is a device with an Internet domain name that can communicate directly or indirectly with the GSTN; mta-I-pstn is the domain name that identifies it; and pstn-email is the complete email address used to carry a GSTN address.
sections.eli5: There were lots of different ways to write a phone number as an email address. This RFC picks one simple way that everyone can agree on.

sections.title: The Minimal pstn-address
sections.content:
A pstn-address is a pstn-mbox optionally followed by qualif-type1 extensions. The mailbox is a service-selector, an equals sign and a global-phone. The selector is made of digits, letters and hyphens, no spaces, and MUST be handled case insensitively.

The global-phone is a + followed by digits, with hyphens or dots allowed as written separators. It represents a standard E.164 numeric address. Separators are allowed to help human readers but are not recommended for transmission, and they MUST be ignored by conforming implementations.

Other dialing schemes, such as private numbering plans, are allowed, but they MUST NOT use the leading +, which is reserved for the standard global-phone syntax. Support for the global-phone syntax remains mandatory.

Extensions have the form /keyword=string. Implementations may ignore extensions they do not understand, but MUST preserve all qualif-type1 elements they receive.
sections.eli5: You write the kind of service (like VOICE or FAX), an equals sign, and the phone number starting with a plus. Extra details can be tacked on after a slash.

sections.title: The Complete pstn-email Address
sections.content:
The right-hand side of the address, after the @, is the mta-I-pstn, the domain name of the gateway. For SMTP transmission it MUST conform to the domain rules of the SMTP and host requirements specifications, and in message headers to the message format standards. Domain names and domain literals are both permitted.

The full address, pstn-email, is the pstn-address with optional surrounding slashes and quotes, then @ and the domain. The optional slashes can come from translations through other gateways such as some X.400 gateways. Implementations MUST accept them but SHOULD NOT generate them.

If a GSTN service needs several subaddresses for the same pstn-mbox, then multiple pstn-email elements are REQUIRED, because email practice uses a separate address for each recipient. A user agent may accept several subaddresses, but MUST generate multiple pstn-mbox elements when submitting to the MTA.
sections.eli5: After the phone part comes the @ sign and the name of the gateway, just like any email. If you want to reach several extensions, you write one address for each.

sections.title: Registering New Elements
sections.content:
Any specification that adopts the pstn-address format MUST define and register a unique case insensitive service-selector with IANA, and MUST register any other qualif-type1 elements it needs. Registrations must meet the "Specification Required" criterion from RFC 2434, so the values and meaning are documented in an RFC or other permanent, readily available reference.

The RFC supplies two registration templates, one for a new service-selector and one for a new qualif-type1 keyword. The second template requires a self-contained ABNF definition of the value and a use restriction (or none). IANA MUST NOT accept registrations without a specification and fully completed templates.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a new kind of service, they must write down how it works and register the name, so nobody else uses the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Email routing depends on DNS data, so a successful attack on DNS could send messages through an MTA or gateway whose software is compromised. The RFC lists ways incorrect routing information might reach a client: compromising a DNS server, forging a response to a query, or returning incorrect additional information in response to an unrelated query.

Clients SHOULD base mail routing only on authoritative answers. Once DNS Security mechanisms become more widely deployed, clients SHOULD use them to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
sections.eli5: If someone tricks the directory that says where to send the mail, your message could end up at the wrong place. So check that the answers come from the real source.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2303
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no technical or major changes from RFC 2303. The updates are clarifications. The old term PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) became GSTN (Global Switched Telephone Network), but the ABNF names kept the old spelling for consistency. The text now says GSTN addresses are, in common language, telephone numbers, and that global-phone represents E.164 numeric addresses.

It also adds the list of new terms, makes the IANA registration duty explicit with templates, clarifies written separators, spells out quoting rules in pstn-email, and explains how to generate pstn-email when more than one subaddress is used.
sections.eli5: This is a tidy-up of the older version. The rules did not really change; the wording got clearer.

viz.caption: ABNF AND EXAMPLE ADDRESSES FROM RFC 3191

data.title: Minimal GSTN address
data.code:
pstn-address = pstn-mbox [ qualif-type1 ]
pstn-mbox = service-selector "=" global-phone
global-phone = "+" 1*( DIGIT / written-sep )
written-sep = ( "-" / "." )
qualif-type1 = "/" keyword "=" string

VOICE=+3940226338@worldvoice.com
FAX=+1.202.7653000/T33S=6377@faxserv.org
/SMS=+33-1-88335215/@telecom.com
